---
title: "Special Functions for Numerical Integration"
---

The numerical machinery of multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) rests on a small library of
special functions, and the analytic shortcuts that occasionally rescue a closed form rest on the same
library. This appendix is the proved reference for those functions. It collects, in one place and with
full derivations, the four objects that Part V calls on repeatedly: the moment generating function of the
normal, which closes the log-link aggregation integral of @thm-log-link-mgf; the error function, the
analyst's name for the normal distribution function and the gateway to its series and tail expansions;
Owen's $T$ function, which evaluates bivariate normal probabilities and, through them, the expected
squared probit needed for probit-link aggregation; and the radical-inverse function, the arithmetic atom
of the Sobol' sequences that drive the quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) integration of @thm-hypercube-integration.
Two further functions that arise in this circle of ideas, the one-probit and two-probit approximations to
the logistic function, are derived here because they turn the otherwise non-elementary logit aggregation
integral of @thm-logit-no-closed-form into an explicit, fast, and surprisingly accurate closed form.

Everything is proved or derived. Where a result is established in the main text we cite it by slug and,
when it sharpens the reference to restate the derivation, reprove it self-contained. Symbols follow
[Notation](/notation.qmd): $\Phi$ and $\phi$ are the standard normal distribution and density functions,
$\mathrm{expit}(z)=e^{z}/(1+e^{z})$ is the inverse logit (also called the logistic sigmoid), $\Phi^{-1}$ is the normal quantile function, and
$M_X(\mathbf{t})=\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top X}]$ is the moment generating function of @def-mgf. Two
standard facts of real analysis are used without proof: the Gaussian normalization
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-t^{2}}\,dt=\sqrt{\pi}$ (equivalently $\int\phi=1$), proved by the polar-
coordinates evaluation of its square, and differentiation under the integral sign, justified by dominated
convergence (@thm-dominated-convergence) whenever a dominating integrable envelope is exhibited, which we
do at each use.

## How to use this appendix {#sec-sf-guide}

*Scope, and what is deliberately left out.* This appendix is the proved reference for the five objects that
the Part V integration machinery calls on: the normal moment generating function, the error function, Owen's
$T$ function, the one- and two-probit approximations to the logistic, and the radical inverse behind the
Sobol' point set. It is not a general catalogue of the special functions of statistics. The gamma function,
its logarithm, the digamma function, and the beta function do appear in Part V, but only as the fixed
normalizing constants of standard likelihoods, for example the log-gamma terms in the Poisson and binomial
log-likelihoods of Chapters 21 and 25; they are classical, are not special to indirect comparison, and are
not reproved here. Everything below, by contrast, is tied to a concrete ML-NMR integration task and is proved
in full.

*A concrete task to keep in mind.* Picture the setting the whole appendix serves. An aggregate-data (AgD)
study arm reports an event count and a summary of its patients, say a mean and variance of age, but no
individual records. The model has a link function $g$, and to predict this arm's event probability the model
must average the individual probability $g^{-1}(\eta)$ over the arm's covariate distribution. The three
regimes below are exactly the three ways that average can be computed, and each is the job of one group of
functions in this appendix.

| Function or object | Section | Feeds (chapter, result) | What it does for the average |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal MGF | @sec-sf-mgf | Chapter 20, @thm-log-link-mgf (catalogue H.6) | gives the log-link average in exact closed form |
| Error function $\operatorname{erf}$, $\operatorname{erfc}$ | @sec-sf-erf | Chapter 22, @thm-hypercube-integration and @thm-inverse-cdf | the special-function form of $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$ applied at every Sobol' node |
| Owen's $T$ | @sec-sf-owen | Chapter 20 probit aggregation @prp-agg-probit-closed-form | supplies the probit second moment $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\eta)^2]$ |
| One- and two-probit approximation | @sec-sf-probit-logit | Chapter 22 logit aggregation @thm-logit-no-closed-form | a fast explicit approximation to the logit average |
| Radical inverse, Sobol' construction | @sec-sf-sobol | Chapters 22 and 25, @thm-hypercube-integration | builds the low-discrepancy points for the general numerical average |

Read the table as a decision tree for the averaging task: the log link is a closed form (the MGF); the
probit link has a closed form for the first moment and an Owen's $T$ closed form for the second; the logit
link has no closed form but an accurate explicit probit approximation; and every remaining case, including
the survival and ordinal likelihood kernels of Chapter 25, is handled by Sobol' quasi-Monte Carlo, whose
points are built from the radical inverse and pushed onto the covariate scale through $\Phi^{-1}$, that is,
through $\operatorname{erf}^{-1}$. The sections are ordered from the easiest regime to the most general, and
they rise in difficulty: the MGF section is short and gentle, the error-function section is moderate, Owen's
$T$ is the hardest section and carries the Plackett partial differential equation, and the Sobol' section is
moderate but dense with quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) vocabulary. A reader who wants only the applied picture can
take the closed forms and the worked examples from each section and leave the digital-net algebra of
@sec-sf-sobol to software.

## The moment generating function of the normal {#sec-sf-mgf}

The moment generating function (MGF) of @def-mgf turns the average of an exponential into an algebraic
expression. Because the log link sends a linear predictor $\eta$ to the mean $e^{\eta}$, and because a
linear predictor in jointly normal covariates is itself normal, the aggregate mean on the log scale is
the expectation of an exponential of a normal, that is, a normal MGF evaluated at $t=1$. This is the one
nonlinear link for which ML-NMR has an exact closed form, and the MGF is the reason.

The name "moment generating" comes from a fact we do not actually use but which explains the terminology:
differentiating $M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]$ a total of $k$ times and setting $t=0$ returns the $k$-th moment
$\mathbb{E}[X^{k}]$, because each derivative brings down one factor of $X$. We exploit the MGF for a different
reason. The log link sets the mean equal to $e^{\eta}$, so an aggregate mean on the log scale is literally
$\mathbb{E}[e^{W}]$ for the (normal) linear predictor $W$; that is the MGF evaluated at $t=1$, not a
derivative at $t=0$. This is why the log link, alone among the common nonlinear links, yields a closed form:
its inverse link is the exponential, and the exponential of a normal is exactly what the normal MGF
integrates.

::: {#thm-normal-mgf}
## Moment generating function of the normal
Let $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ be univariate normal. Then the MGF of $X$ is finite for every
$t\in\mathbb{R}$ and
$$
M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{tX}\big]=\exp\!\Big(\mu t+\tfrac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}\Big).
$$ {#eq-sf-normal-mgf}
More generally, let $\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ be $p$-variate
normal with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succeq 0$ (positive semidefinite). Then for every $\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$,
$$
M_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{t})=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{X}}\big]
=\exp\!\Big(\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}+\tfrac12\,\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{t}\Big).
$$ {#eq-sf-mvn-mgf}
:::

::: {.proof}
*Univariate case.* Fix $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Writing the density of $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ and
collecting the exponent,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{tX}\big]
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{tx}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\,
e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}\,dx
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\!\Big(-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}-2\sigma^{2}tx}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big)\,dx .
$$
Complete the square in $x$. The numerator of the exponent is
$$
(x-\mu)^{2}-2\sigma^{2}tx
=\big(x-(\mu+\sigma^{2}t)\big)^{2}-2\sigma^{2}t\mu-\sigma^{4}t^{2},
$$
which one verifies by expanding the completed square,
$\big(x-(\mu+\sigma^{2}t)\big)^{2}=x^{2}-2\mu x-2\sigma^{2}tx+\mu^{2}+2\mu\sigma^{2}t+\sigma^{4}t^{2}$: then
subtracting the two constants $2\sigma^{2}t\mu$ and $\sigma^{4}t^{2}$ cancels the final two terms and leaves
$x^{2}-2\mu x-2\sigma^{2}tx+\mu^{2}=(x-\mu)^{2}-2\sigma^{2}tx$, the left side. Substituting and factoring out
the constant terms,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{tX}\big]
=e^{\mu t+\frac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}}\cdot
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
e^{-\frac{(x-(\mu+\sigma^{2}t))^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}\,dx
=e^{\mu t+\frac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}},
$$
the remaining integral being that of a $\mathcal{N}(\mu+\sigma^{2}t,\sigma^{2})$ density, which equals
$1$. The expectation is finite for every $t$ because the integrand is a positive constant times a Gaussian
density. This is @eq-sf-normal-mgf.

*Multivariate case.* The law $\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ is defined in @def-mvn
through exactly the MGF @eq-sf-mvn-mgf, so the statement is the consistency of that definition, which we
reprove for reference. Let $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ be the symmetric positive semidefinite square root
of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ (@thm-spectral-theorem), let $\mathbf{Z}=(Z_1,\dots,Z_p)^\top$ have independent
standard normal entries, and set $\mathbf{X}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}$, which
has mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and, since $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$ is symmetric with
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, covariance
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}I_p\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
By independence and the univariate MGF $\mathbb{E}[e^{sZ_i}]=e^{s^{2}/2}$ from @eq-sf-normal-mgf,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{X}}\big]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}}\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{E}\big[e^{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t})_i Z_i}\big]
=e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}}\exp\!\Big(\tfrac12\big\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}\big\|_2^{2}\Big)
=\exp\!\Big(\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}\Big),
$$
using $\|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}\|_2^{2}=\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}$.
This is @eq-sf-mvn-mgf, identical to @eq-mvn-mgf. $\square$
:::

*Reader's translation.* @eq-sf-normal-mgf says the average of $e^{tX}$ over a normal $X$ is itself an
exponential, with the variance entering through the quadratic $\tfrac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}$. That single formula
is the entire reason the log-link aggregate mean has a closed form; the next corollary reads it off at $t=1$.

The aggregation payoff is immediate. An aggregate mean on the log scale is the expectation of an
exponential of a linear predictor; when the covariates are jointly normal the linear predictor is normal,
and @eq-sf-normal-mgf evaluates the expectation at $t=1$.

::: {#cor-sf-log-link}
## Closed-form log-link aggregation
Let the inverse link be $g^{-1}(z)=e^{z}$ (the log link) and let the covariates in study $j$ be jointly
normal, $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)$. Write
$\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_1+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}$ for the total slope on
arm $k$ and $W=\eta_{jk}(X)=\mu_j+\gamma_k+X^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}$ for the linear
predictor. Then $W\sim\mathcal{N}(m,v)$ with
$$
m=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k},
\qquad
v=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\,\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k},
$$
and the aggregate mean is
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{W}\big]=M_W(1)=\exp\!\Big(m+\tfrac12 v\Big)
=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\cdot e^{\,v/2},
\qquad
\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=e^{m}.
$$ {#eq-sf-log-link}
This is the closed form @eq-agg-log-mgf of @thm-log-link-mgf; the multiplicative correction $e^{v/2}\ge 1$
is the exact downward bias of the plug-in mean, with equality if and only if
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=\mathbf{0}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The linear predictor $W$ is an affine function of the normal vector $X$, hence univariate normal by the
affine-image theorem @thm-mvn-linear, with the stated mean $m$ and variance
$v=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}$. The
aggregate mean of @def-aggregate-model is $\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb{E}[g^{-1}(W)]=\mathbb{E}[e^{W}]$,
which is $M_W(1)$ by @def-mgf. Evaluating @eq-sf-normal-mgf at $t=1$ gives
$M_W(1)=\exp(m+\tfrac12 v)$. Finally $e^{m+v/2}=e^{m}e^{v/2}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}e^{v/2}$,
and $v\ge 0$ because $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\succeq 0$ (@thm-cov-psd), with $v=0$ exactly when
$\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}$ lies in the null space of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$. $\square$
:::

::: {#exm-sf-log-link}
## A multivariate log-link aggregate by hand
Take two covariates, $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)$ with
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j=(2,1)^\top$ and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0.5\\0.5&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, total slope
$\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=(0.4,0.3)^\top$, and intercept-plus-treatment $\mu_j+\gamma_k=-1$.
The mean linear predictor is
$m=-1+\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=-1+(2)(0.4)+(1)(0.3)=0.1$. The variance is
the quadratic form
$$
v=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}
=(0.4,0.3)\begin{pmatrix}0.55\\0.80\end{pmatrix}=(0.4)(0.55)+(0.3)(0.80)=0.46,
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{tot},k}=(0.55,0.80)^\top$. By @eq-sf-log-link the
exact aggregate rate is $\theta_{\bullet jk}=e^{0.1+0.23}=e^{0.33}=1.3910$, against the plug-in
$\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=e^{0.1}=1.1052$. The covariance off-diagonal enters only through $v$:
the same margins with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ diagonal would give $v=(0.16)(1)+(0.09)(2)=0.34$ and
$\theta_{\bullet jk}=e^{0.27}=1.3100$, so the positive covariance inflates the aggregate by the factor
$e^{(0.46-0.34)/2}=e^{0.06}=1.0618$. The MGF makes the dependence on the full covariance matrix exact and
explicit. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The error function {#sec-sf-erf}

The normal distribution function has no elementary antiderivative, so numerical analysis works with a
rescaled, standardized version of it called the error function. Numerical libraries evaluate $\Phi$ and
$\Phi^{-1}$ by rational approximations of $\operatorname{erf}$-type functions, and the series and asymptotic
expansions of the error function are the practical tools for evaluating tail probabilities and normal
quantiles.

This is not decorative. In the Chapter 22 integration pipeline every Sobol' node is a point $u\in(0,1)$ that
must be pushed onto the covariate scale through the normal quantile $\Phi^{-1}(u)$ (the inverse-CDF transform
of @thm-inverse-cdf), which equals $\sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(2u-1)$. Every normal
probability the fitted model reports, including the small tail probabilities that arise for rare events, is
computed as an $\operatorname{erf}$ or $\operatorname{erfc}$ value. Stable evaluation of these functions is
therefore part of what makes the integration numerically reliable, which is why they earn a section of their
own rather than hiding inside a call to $\Phi$.

::: {#def-error-function}
## Error function and complementary error function
The **error function** is
$$
\operatorname{erf}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_{0}^{x}e^{-t^{2}}\,dt,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},
$$ {#eq-sf-erf-def}
and the **complementary error function** is
$\operatorname{erfc}(x)=1-\operatorname{erf}(x)=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\displaystyle\int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t^{2}}\,dt$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader's translation.* The error function is the normal distribution function in disguise: it integrates the
same Gaussian bump $e^{-t^{2}}$, but centered at $0$, scaled so that $\operatorname{erf}(\pm\infty)=\pm1$,
and measured from the center outward. The complement $\operatorname{erfc}=1-\operatorname{erf}$ is what you
use when the interesting probability is a small tail, because it is computed directly instead of by
subtracting two nearly equal numbers.

::: {#prp-erf-phi}
## The error function and the normal distribution function
The error function is odd, $\operatorname{erf}(-x)=-\operatorname{erf}(x)$, with $\operatorname{erf}(0)=0$
and $\operatorname{erf}(\pm\infty)=\pm 1$. It is related to the standard normal distribution function by
$$
\Phi(x)=\frac12\Big(1+\operatorname{erf}\!\big(x/\sqrt{2}\big)\Big)
=\frac12\operatorname{erfc}\!\big(-x/\sqrt{2}\big),
\qquad
\operatorname{erf}(x)=2\Phi\!\big(x\sqrt{2}\big)-1,
$$ {#eq-sf-erf-phi}
and the quantile functions are related by
$$
\Phi^{-1}(p)=\sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(2p-1),\qquad p\in(0,1).
$$ {#eq-sf-erfinv-phiinv}
The densities satisfy $\phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2}$ and
$\operatorname{erf}'(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-x^{2}}$, consistent with @eq-sf-erf-phi by the chain rule.
:::

::: {.proof}
Oddness is immediate from @eq-sf-erf-def, since $t\mapsto e^{-t^{2}}$ is even, so reversing the sign of the
upper limit reverses the sign of the integral; $\operatorname{erf}(0)=0$ is the empty integral, and
$\operatorname{erf}(+\infty)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^\infty e^{-t^2}\,dt=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\cdot\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}=1$
by the Gaussian normalization, with $\operatorname{erf}(-\infty)=-1$ by oddness.

For @eq-sf-erf-phi, start from $\Phi(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}\phi(u)\,du=\frac12+\int_{0}^{x}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^{2}/2}\,du$,
the constant $\frac12$ being $\Phi(0)$ by the symmetry of $\phi$. Substitute $u=\sqrt{2}\,t$, so
$du=\sqrt{2}\,dt$ and the upper limit becomes $x/\sqrt{2}$:
$$
\Phi(x)=\frac12+\int_{0}^{x/\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-t^{2}}\sqrt{2}\,dt
=\frac12+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_{0}^{x/\sqrt{2}}e^{-t^{2}}\,dt
=\frac12+\frac12\operatorname{erf}\!\big(x/\sqrt{2}\big),
$$
using $\frac{1}{\sqrt\pi}=\frac12\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}$ to recognize @eq-sf-erf-def. This is the first
equality of @eq-sf-erf-phi; the second is $\operatorname{erf}=1-\operatorname{erfc}$ together with
oddness, and inverting $p=\frac12(1+\operatorname{erf}(x/\sqrt2))$ for $x$ gives @eq-sf-erfinv-phiinv. The
density identity $\operatorname{erf}'(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}e^{-x^{2}}$ is the fundamental theorem of
calculus applied to @eq-sf-erf-def, and differentiating @eq-sf-erf-phi reproduces
$\phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\cdot\frac12\operatorname{erf}'(x/\sqrt2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the error function does in health statistics.** Every normal probability a health technology
assessment (HTA) reports is an error-function value in disguise. Three tasks recur.

| Health-statistics task | Function used |
|---|---|
| a normal $p$-value or a confidence-limit tail | $\Phi$, $\operatorname{erfc}$ |
| turning a Sobol' uniform $u$ into a normal covariate | $\Phi^{-1}$, hence $\operatorname{erf}^{-1}$ |
| avoiding numerical underflow in an extreme tail | $\operatorname{erfc}$ or $\operatorname{erfcx}$ |

For a concrete instance, the familiar two-sided $95\%$ cutoff $1.96$ satisfies, by @eq-sf-erf-phi,
$\Phi(1.96)=\tfrac12\big(1+\operatorname{erf}(1.96/\sqrt2)\big)=\tfrac12\big(1+\operatorname{erf}(1.3859)\big)=\tfrac12(1+0.9500)=0.9750$,
and the upper tail is
$1-\Phi(1.96)=\tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}(1.3859)=\tfrac12(0.0500)=0.0250$. The tail form earns its keep far
out: $1-\Phi(10)=\tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}(10/\sqrt2)\approx 7.6\times10^{-24}$ is returned accurately by
$\operatorname{erfc}$, whereas forming $\Phi(10)\approx 1$ first and subtracting would return $0$ by
cancellation. This is the sense in which the tail-safe functions are part of the pipeline, not an ornament.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

For evaluation one needs a convergent series near the origin and an asymptotic expansion in the tail. Both
follow from @eq-sf-erf-def by elementary calculus.

::: {#prp-erf-expansions}
## Series and tail expansions
The error function has the everywhere-convergent Maclaurin series
$$
\operatorname{erf}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}x^{2n+1}}{n!\,(2n+1)}
=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(x-\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{x^{5}}{10}-\frac{x^{7}}{42}+\cdots\Big),
$$ {#eq-sf-erf-series}
and the complementary error function has the asymptotic expansion, as $x\to+\infty$,
$$
\operatorname{erfc}(x)=\frac{e^{-x^{2}}}{x\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(1-\frac{1}{2x^{2}}+\frac{3}{4x^{4}}-\cdots\Big),
$$ {#eq-sf-erfc-asymptotic}
which translates, through @eq-sf-erf-phi, into the normal-tail statement (the Mills ratio is the
tail-to-density ratio $(1-\Phi(x))/\phi(x)$)
$1-\Phi(x)=\phi(x)\big(\tfrac{1}{x}-\tfrac{1}{x^{3}}+\tfrac{3}{x^{5}}-\cdots\big)$ as $x\to+\infty$, so in
particular $1-\Phi(x)\sim\phi(x)/x$, where the symbol $\sim$ means the ratio of the two sides tends to $1$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The series @eq-sf-erf-series is the termwise integration of the everywhere-convergent power series
$e^{-t^{2}}=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^{n}t^{2n}/n!$, legitimate because the series converges uniformly on every
bounded interval; integrating $t^{2n}$ from $0$ to $x$ gives $x^{2n+1}/(2n+1)$ and the factor
$\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}$ from @eq-sf-erf-def.

For @eq-sf-erfc-asymptotic, integrate by parts in
$\operatorname{erfc}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_x^\infty e^{-t^{2}}\,dt$, writing
$e^{-t^{2}}=\frac{1}{-2t}\,\frac{d}{dt}e^{-t^{2}}$:
$$
\int_x^\infty e^{-t^{2}}\,dt
=\Big[-\frac{e^{-t^{2}}}{2t}\Big]_x^\infty-\int_x^\infty\frac{e^{-t^{2}}}{2t^{2}}\,dt
=\frac{e^{-x^{2}}}{2x}-\frac12\int_x^\infty\frac{e^{-t^{2}}}{t^{2}}\,dt .
$$
Iterating the same step on the remainder integral generates the alternating series in inverse powers of
$x$; the expansion is asymptotic rather than convergent because the integrated-by-parts remainder, after
$N$ steps, is bounded by a constant times $e^{-x^{2}}x^{-(2N+1)}$, which is smaller than the last retained
term but does not tend to zero as $N\to\infty$ at fixed $x$. Multiplying by $\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}$ gives
@eq-sf-erfc-asymptotic. The Mills ratio statement is @eq-sf-erfc-asymptotic rewritten through
$1-\Phi(x)=\frac12\operatorname{erfc}(x/\sqrt2)$ and $\phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2}$:
substituting $x\mapsto x/\sqrt2$ and simplifying $\frac12\cdot\frac{e^{-x^{2}/2}}{(x/\sqrt2)\sqrt\pi}=\frac{e^{-x^{2}/2}}{x\sqrt{2\pi}}=\phi(x)/x$
identifies the leading term, and the subsequent coefficients follow likewise. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Convergent versus asymptotic, and why the tail series is still useful.** The two expansions of
@prp-erf-expansions behave oppositely. The Maclaurin series @eq-sf-erf-series is *convergent*: fix $x$, keep
adding terms, and the partial sums approach $\operatorname{erf}(x)$ without limit, so more terms always mean
more accuracy. The tail expansion @eq-sf-erfc-asymptotic is *asymptotic*: for a fixed large $x$ the terms
first shrink, reach a smallest term, and then grow, so the series diverges if pushed too far. One uses it by
stopping at the smallest term, which for large $x$ already gives extraordinary accuracy. The practical rule
is: near the origin use the convergent series, in the tail truncate the asymptotic series at its smallest
term. This is exactly how library routines for $\Phi$ and $\operatorname{erfc}$ switch regimes.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why software standardizes on $\operatorname{erf}$.** The change of variable $u=\sqrt2\,t$ that produced
@eq-sf-erf-phi is the only difference between $\Phi$ and $\operatorname{erf}$: they are the same function
up to an affine rescaling of the argument and the range. Numerical libraries implement
$\operatorname{erf}$, $\operatorname{erfc}$, and $\operatorname{erf}^{-1}$ as primitives, often with the
scaled complement $\operatorname{erfcx}(x)=e^{x^{2}}\operatorname{erfc}(x)$ to avoid overflow in the tail,
and obtain $\Phi$, $1-\Phi$, and $\Phi^{-1}$ by @eq-sf-erf-phi and @eq-sf-erfinv-phiinv. Every appearance
of $\Phi$ or $\Phi^{-1}$ in the ML-NMR pipeline of @thm-hypercube-integration, in the Gaussian copula
@eq-qmc-gaussian-copula, and in the inverse-CDF transform @thm-inverse-cdf, is computed this way.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Owen's $T$ function {#sec-sf-owen}

The error function evaluates one-dimensional normal integrals. The two-dimensional analogue, the bivariate
normal probability, has no reduction to a single error function; the irreducible new ingredient is Owen's
$T$ function (@owen1956). We define it, give its probabilistic meaning, prove the bivariate normal
probability identity that motivated Owen's tables, and then prove the identity for the expected squared
normal distribution function that probit-link aggregation needs.

Before the formal definition, here is the picture and the purpose, because both are easy to lose once the
integral appears.

*The picture.* Owen's $T$ measures the probability that a random point lands in a wedge. Take two independent
standard normal draws $X$ and $Y$ and plot the point $(X,Y)$ in the plane. Owen's $T(h,a)$, for $h\ge 0$ and
$a\ge 0$, is the chance that this point falls into the wedge bounded on the left by the vertical line at $h$
and above by the ray $Y=aX$ through the origin, the region $\{X>h,\ 0<Y<aX\}$. So $h$ sets a vertical cutoff
for the first variable and $a$ sets the slope of the sloped edge for the second: larger $h$ pushes the wedge
to the right and shrinks it, larger $a$ tilts the sloped edge upward and enlarges it. The integral in the
definition below is simply the analytic formula for the normal-probability content of that wedge.

*The purpose.* We need this wedge because of probit aggregation. When the link is the probit, the aggregate
binomial likelihood of an AgD arm depends on the response through both its mean and its variance, and a
Bernoulli response with success probability $\Phi(\eta)$ has variance $\Phi(\eta)(1-\Phi(\eta))$. Averaging
over the covariate distribution, the aggregate needs both the first moment $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\eta)]$, which
@prp-agg-probit-closed-form gives as a single $\Phi$, and the second moment $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\eta)^{2}]$. That
second moment turns out to be a bivariate normal probability, and Owen's $T$ is precisely the function that
reduces a bivariate normal probability to a one-dimensional integral. This is why the error function, which
handled one-dimensional normal integrals, cannot finish the job alone.

*One analytic signpost.* Several proofs below differentiate under the integral sign, meaning they move a
derivative inside an integral. This is a genuine theorem, not a formality: it is licensed whenever the
integrand's derivative is bounded by a fixed integrable function (a dominating envelope), which we display at
each use. A reader can treat each such step as permitted once the envelope is shown.

::: {#def-owens-t}
## Owen's $T$ function
For $h\in\mathbb{R}$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$, **Owen's $T$ function** is
$$
T(h,a)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\exp\!\big(-\tfrac12 h^{2}(1+x^{2})\big)}{1+x^{2}}\,dx .
$$ {#eq-sf-owens-t-def}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Three structural facts are read directly off @eq-sf-owens-t-def: $T(h,0)=0$ for all $h$; $T(h,a)=T(-h,a)$,
because the integrand depends on $h$ only through $h^{2}$, so $T(h,a)=T(|h|,a)$; and $T(h,-a)=-T(h,a)$ by
reversing the limits. The next lemma gives the probabilistic content.

::: {#lem-owens-t-representation}
## Integral and probabilistic representation
For all $h\in\mathbb{R}$ and $a\ge 0$,
$$
T(h,a)=\int_{h}^{\infty}\phi(x)\,\Big(\Phi(ax)-\tfrac12\Big)\,dx .
$$ {#eq-sf-owens-t-rep}
If moreover $h\ge 0$, then $T(h,a)$ is the probability that two independent standard normals
$X,Y\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ fall in the wedge $\{X>h,\ 0<Y<aX\}$:
$$
T(h,a)=P\big(X>h,\ 0<Y<aX\big),\qquad h\ge 0,\ a\ge 0 .
$$ {#eq-sf-owens-t-prob}
:::

::: {.proof}
Both sides of @eq-sf-owens-t-rep vanish at $a=0$: the left by $T(h,0)=0$, the right because
$\Phi(0)-\frac12=0$. It therefore suffices to show their derivatives in $a$ agree for $a>0$. The left side,
by the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to the upper limit of @eq-sf-owens-t-def,
$$
\partial_a T(h,a)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\,\frac{e^{-\frac12 h^{2}(1+a^{2})}}{1+a^{2}} .
$$ {#eq-sf-owens-t-da}
For the right side, differentiate under the integral (the integrand's $a$-derivative
$\phi(x)\,x\,\phi(ax)$ is dominated by the integrable $|x|\phi(x)\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$):
$$
\partial_a\int_h^\infty\phi(x)\big(\Phi(ax)-\tfrac12\big)\,dx
=\int_h^\infty\phi(x)\,x\,\phi(ax)\,dx
=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_h^\infty x\,e^{-\frac12 x^{2}(1+a^{2})}\,dx .
$$
The last integral is elementary: an antiderivative of $x\,e^{-\frac12 x^{2}(1+a^{2})}$ is
$-\frac{1}{1+a^{2}}e^{-\frac12 x^{2}(1+a^{2})}$, which vanishes at $+\infty$ and equals
$-\frac{1}{1+a^{2}}e^{-\frac12 h^{2}(1+a^{2})}$ at $x=h$, for every real $h$. Hence the integral equals
$\frac{1}{1+a^{2}}e^{-\frac12 h^{2}(1+a^{2})}$, and the derivative of the right side is
$\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{e^{-\frac12 h^{2}(1+a^{2})}}{1+a^{2}}$, matching @eq-sf-owens-t-da. The two sides of
@eq-sf-owens-t-rep agree at $a=0$ and have equal derivatives, so they are equal for all $a\ge 0$.

For @eq-sf-owens-t-prob with $h\ge 0$, observe that for $x>h\ge 0$ the inner probability
$P(0<Y<ax)=\Phi(ax)-\Phi(0)=\Phi(ax)-\frac12$ is the genuine probability of the interval $(0,ax)$, so
$$
P(X>h,\ 0<Y<aX)=\int_h^\infty\phi(x)\,P(0<Y<ax)\,dx=\int_h^\infty\phi(x)\big(\Phi(ax)-\tfrac12\big)\,dx
=T(h,a)
$$
by @eq-sf-owens-t-rep. (For $h<0$ the same integral @eq-sf-owens-t-rep remains valid as an analytic
identity, but its integrand is negative on $(h,0)$ and it is no longer the probability of a wedge.) $\square$
:::

Two special values follow at once and will be needed below.

::: {#lem-owens-t-special}
## Special values of Owen's $T$
For every $h\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$
T(h,1)=\tfrac12\,\Phi(h)\big(1-\Phi(h)\big),
\qquad
\lim_{a\to\infty}T(h,a)=\tfrac12\big(1-\Phi(|h|)\big).
$$ {#eq-sf-owens-t-special}
:::

::: {.proof}
Set $a=1$ in @eq-sf-owens-t-rep: $T(h,1)=\int_h^\infty\phi(x)\big(\Phi(x)-\tfrac12\big)\,dx
=\int_h^\infty\phi(x)\Phi(x)\,dx-\tfrac12\int_h^\infty\phi(x)\,dx$. In the first integral,
$\frac{d}{dx}\big[\tfrac12\Phi(x)^{2}\big]=\Phi(x)\phi(x)$, so
$\int_h^\infty\phi\Phi=\tfrac12\Phi(x)^{2}\big|_h^\infty=\tfrac12\big(1-\Phi(h)^{2}\big)$; the second is
$\tfrac12\big(1-\Phi(h)\big)$. Subtracting,
$T(h,1)=\tfrac12(1-\Phi(h)^{2})-\tfrac12(1-\Phi(h))=\tfrac12\Phi(h)\big(1-\Phi(h)\big)$. For the limit, use
$T(h,a)=T(|h|,a)$ and @eq-sf-owens-t-prob with $|h|\ge 0$: as $a\to\infty$ the wedge $\{X>|h|,0<Y<aX\}$
increases to $\{X>|h|,Y>0\}$, whose probability is $P(X>|h|)P(Y>0)=\big(1-\Phi(|h|)\big)\cdot\tfrac12$ by
independence. $\square$
:::

The bridge from Owen's $T$ to bivariate normal probabilities is a classical partial differential equation
for the bivariate normal density, due to Plackett: the density's derivative in the correlation equals its
mixed second derivative in the two coordinates.

Why differentiate in the correlation $\rho$? Because it lets us build the bivariate probability we want out
of a case we already know. At $\rho=0$ the two coordinates are independent and the joint probability
factorizes into $\Phi(\lambda)^{2}$; at the target $\rho$ it is the quantity we are after. Sliding $\rho$
continuously from $0$ to its target and accumulating the change reduces the unknown probability to an
integral of its $\rho$-derivative. Plackett's identity @eq-sf-biv-pde is what makes this tractable: it says
that $\rho$-derivative is nothing but the corner value of the density, a quantity we can write down
explicitly. The lemma is the engine; the theorem after it turns the crank.

::: {#lem-bivariate-normal-pde}
## The correlation heat equation for the bivariate normal
Let $f(x,y;\rho)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}\exp\!\Big(-\dfrac{x^{2}-2\rho xy+y^{2}}{2(1-\rho^{2})}\Big)$
be the standard bivariate normal density with correlation $\rho\in(-1,1)$. Then
$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\rho}=\frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x\,\partial y}.
$$ {#eq-sf-biv-pde}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $D=1-\rho^{2}$, $Q=x^{2}-2\rho xy+y^{2}$, and $g=e^{-Q/(2D)}$, so $f=(2\pi)^{-1}D^{-1/2}g$. For the
right side, $\partial_x g=g\cdot\big(-(x-\rho y)/D\big)$ and then
$$
\partial_y\partial_x g
=g\Big(-\tfrac{y-\rho x}{D}\Big)\Big(-\tfrac{x-\rho y}{D}\Big)+g\cdot\tfrac{\rho}{D}
=g\Big[\tfrac{(x-\rho y)(y-\rho x)}{D^{2}}+\tfrac{\rho}{D}\Big],
$$
so $\partial_x\partial_y f=(2\pi)^{-1}D^{-1/2}g\big[(x-\rho y)(y-\rho x)/D^{2}+\rho/D\big]$. For the left
side, $\partial_\rho D^{-1/2}=\rho D^{-3/2}$ and, since $\partial_\rho Q=-2xy$,
$\partial_\rho g=g\,\partial_\rho(-Q/2D)=g\big(xy/D-\rho Q/D^{2}\big)$, whence
$\partial_\rho f=(2\pi)^{-1}D^{-1/2}g\big[\rho/D+xy/D-\rho Q/D^{2}\big]$. The two expressions agree if and
only if $xyD-\rho Q=(x-\rho y)(y-\rho x)$. Expanding both sides,
$$
(x-\rho y)(y-\rho x)=(1+\rho^{2})xy-\rho(x^{2}+y^{2}),\qquad
xyD-\rho Q=(1-\rho^{2})xy-\rho(x^{2}-2\rho xy+y^{2})=(1+\rho^{2})xy-\rho(x^{2}+y^{2}),
$$
which are equal. $\square$
:::

We can now prove the bivariate normal probability identity on the diagonal, which is exactly the case
probit aggregation requires.

::: {#thm-owens-t-identity}
## Bivariate normal probability via Owen's $T$
Let $(V_1,V_2)$ be standard bivariate normal with correlation $\rho\in(-1,1)$, and let $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.
Then
$$
P\big(V_1\le\lambda,\ V_2\le\lambda\big)
=\Phi(\lambda)-2\,T\!\Big(\lambda,\ \sqrt{\tfrac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}}\Big).
$$ {#eq-sf-owens-t-identity}
:::

*Roadmap for the proof.* The strategy is the deformation just described. Both sides are checked to agree at
$\rho=0$ (the independent base case, where the probability is $\Phi(\lambda)^{2}$), and then both sides are
shown to have the same derivative in $\rho$. Two functions that start equal and change at the same rate stay
equal, so they coincide for every $\rho$. The one technical point is a change of variable
$a(\rho)=\sqrt{(1-\rho)/(1+\rho)}$ that carries $\rho$ into the second argument of $T$; the checkpoint
$1+a(\rho)^{2}=2/(1+\rho)$ is what makes the algebra collapse.

::: {.proof}
Write $\Psi(\rho)=P(V_1\le\lambda,V_2\le\lambda)=\int_{-\infty}^{\lambda}\int_{-\infty}^{\lambda}f(x,y;\rho)\,dx\,dy$
for fixed $\lambda$. Differentiating in $\rho$ and using @eq-sf-biv-pde,
$$
\Psi'(\rho)=\int_{-\infty}^{\lambda}\int_{-\infty}^{\lambda}\partial_\rho f\,dx\,dy
=\int_{-\infty}^{\lambda}\int_{-\infty}^{\lambda}\partial_x\partial_y f\,dx\,dy
=f(\lambda,\lambda;\rho),
$$
the double integral of the mixed derivative collapsing by the fundamental theorem of calculus in each
variable, since $f$ and its first derivatives vanish as either argument tends to $-\infty$. Evaluating the
density on the diagonal, with $x^{2}-2\rho xy+y^{2}=2\lambda^{2}(1-\rho)$ at $x=y=\lambda$ and
$1-\rho^{2}=(1-\rho)(1+\rho)$,
$$
f(\lambda,\lambda;\rho)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{2\lambda^{2}(1-\rho)}{2(1-\rho^{2})}\Big)
=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}\,e^{-\lambda^{2}/(1+\rho)} .
$$ {#eq-sf-biv-diagonal}
At $\rho=0$ the coordinates are independent, so $\Psi(0)=\Phi(\lambda)^{2}$, and by
@eq-sf-owens-t-special the base case can be written
$\Psi(0)=\Phi(\lambda)-2T(\lambda,1)$, since $2T(\lambda,1)=\Phi(\lambda)(1-\Phi(\lambda))$ gives
$\Phi(\lambda)-2T(\lambda,1)=\Phi(\lambda)\Phi(\lambda)=\Phi(\lambda)^2$. Define
$a(\rho)=\sqrt{(1-\rho)/(1+\rho)}$, a decreasing bijection from $(-1,1)$ onto $(0,\infty)$ with $a(0)=1$.
We claim $G(\rho):=\Phi(\lambda)-2T(\lambda,a(\rho))$ has the same derivative as $\Psi$ and the same value at
$\rho=0$, hence equals $\Psi$ throughout.

The value at $\rho=0$ matches by construction. For the derivative, by the chain rule and @eq-sf-owens-t-da,
$$
G'(\rho)=-2\,\partial_a T(\lambda,a)\big|_{a=a(\rho)}\,a'(\rho)
=-2\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{e^{-\frac12\lambda^{2}(1+a(\rho)^{2})}}{1+a(\rho)^{2}}\cdot a'(\rho).
$$
Now $1+a^{2}=1+\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}=\frac{2}{1+\rho}$, so $\frac12\lambda^{2}(1+a^{2})=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{1+\rho}$
and $\frac{1}{1+a^{2}}=\frac{1+\rho}{2}$. Differentiating $a(\rho)^{2}=(1-\rho)/(1+\rho)$ gives
$2a\,a'=\frac{-(1+\rho)-(1-\rho)}{(1+\rho)^{2}}=\frac{-2}{(1+\rho)^{2}}$, so
$a'(\rho)=\frac{-1}{a(1+\rho)^{2}}$ with $a=\sqrt{(1-\rho)/(1+\rho)}$, that is
$a'(\rho)=\frac{-1}{(1+\rho)^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}}=\frac{-1}{(1+\rho)^{3/2}(1-\rho)^{1/2}}=\frac{-1}{(1+\rho)\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}$.
Substituting,
$$
G'(\rho)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\,e^{-\lambda^{2}/(1+\rho)}\cdot\frac{1+\rho}{2}\cdot\frac{-1}{(1+\rho)\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}
=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}\,e^{-\lambda^{2}/(1+\rho)}=f(\lambda,\lambda;\rho)=\Psi'(\rho),
$$
matching @eq-sf-biv-diagonal. Since $G$ and $\Psi$ agree at $\rho=0$ and have equal derivatives on
$(-1,1)$, they are equal, which is @eq-sf-owens-t-identity. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Where this identity is used, and where it is not.** @eq-sf-owens-t-identity is the workhorse behind the
probit second moment of the next theorem, and it is the right tool whenever one needs an analytic bivariate
normal probability, for instance to check a probit-link fit by hand. It is not needed to generate the
quasi-Monte Carlo covariate nodes of Chapter 22: sampling from a Gaussian copula requires only the marginal
quantile $\Phi^{-1}$, not the bivariate distribution function, so ML-NMR fitting never evaluates the full
copula CDF. The identity explains and checks the bivariate object; it does not sit on the sampling path.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The general Owen reduction.** Off the diagonal, the same differentiate-in-$\rho$ argument yields Owen's
general formula for the standard bivariate normal distribution function $\Phi_2(h,k;\rho)=P(V_1\le h,V_2\le k)$,
$$
\Phi_2(h,k;\rho)=\tfrac12\Phi(h)+\tfrac12\Phi(k)
-T\!\Big(h,\tfrac{k-\rho h}{h\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}\Big)
-T\!\Big(k,\tfrac{h-\rho k}{k\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}\Big)-\varepsilon,
$$ {#eq-sf-owen-general}
where $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$ when exactly one of $h,k$ is negative and $\varepsilon=0$ otherwise; this is
the identity that Owen's tables (@owen1956) tabulate, and @eq-sf-owens-t-identity is its specialization to
$h=k=\lambda$, where the two $T$-terms coincide and $\varepsilon=0$. We use only the diagonal case, which
we have proved in full; the general formula is stated for reference. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The probit-link aggregate likelihood needs not only the first moment of a probit response, the closed form
$\mathbb{E}[\Phi(a+bZ)]=\Phi(a/\sqrt{1+b^{2}})$ of @prp-agg-probit-closed-form, but also its second
moment, which Owen's $T$ supplies.

::: {#thm-expected-squared-probit}
## Expected squared normal distribution function
Let $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. With $\lambda=a/\sqrt{1+b^{2}}$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\Phi(a+bZ)^{2}\big]
=\Phi(\lambda)-2\,T\!\Big(\lambda,\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2b^{2}}}\Big).
$$ {#eq-sf-expected-squared-probit}
Consequently the variance contribution $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(a+bZ)(1-\Phi(a+bZ))]$, the response-scale
Bernoulli variance averaged over the linear predictor, equals
$\Phi(\lambda)-\mathbb{E}[\Phi(a+bZ)^{2}]=2\,T\big(\lambda,1/\sqrt{1+2b^{2}}\big)$.
:::

*Roadmap for the proof.* The key move is to read a squared probability as a joint probability. Since
$\Phi(a+bZ)$ is itself the probability that a fresh standard normal $U$ falls below $a+bZ$, its square is the
probability that two independent such draws $U_1,U_2$ both fall below $a+bZ$. Both comparisons share the same
random threshold $a+bZ$, so once we average over $Z$ the two draws become correlated through their common
dependence on $Z$. That turns $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(a+bZ)^{2}]$ into a bivariate normal probability, which
@thm-owens-t-identity has already evaluated. In three words: square, condition, correlate.

::: {.proof}
Let $U_1,U_2,Z$ be independent standard normals. For fixed $Z$, the definition of $\Phi$ gives
$\Phi(a+bZ)=P(U_i\le a+bZ\mid Z)$ for each $i$, and by conditional independence of $U_1,U_2$,
$$
\Phi(a+bZ)^{2}=P\big(U_1\le a+bZ,\ U_2\le a+bZ\mid Z\big).
$$
Taking expectations over $Z$ and rearranging the inequalities,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\Phi(a+bZ)^{2}\big]=P\big(U_1-bZ\le a,\ U_2-bZ\le a\big).
$$
The pair $(W_1,W_2)=(U_1-bZ,U_2-bZ)$ is bivariate normal with mean $\mathbf{0}$, equal variances
$\mathrm{Var}(W_i)=1+b^{2}$, and covariance $\mathrm{Cov}(W_1,W_2)=b^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}(Z)=b^{2}$, hence
correlation $\rho=b^{2}/(1+b^{2})$. Standardizing, $V_i=W_i/\sqrt{1+b^{2}}$ are standard normal with
correlation $\rho$, and $P(W_1\le a,W_2\le a)=P(V_1\le\lambda,V_2\le\lambda)$ with
$\lambda=a/\sqrt{1+b^{2}}$. By @thm-owens-t-identity,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\Phi(a+bZ)^{2}\big]=\Phi(\lambda)-2\,T\!\Big(\lambda,\sqrt{\tfrac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}}\Big).
$$
Finally $\dfrac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}=\dfrac{1-\frac{b^{2}}{1+b^{2}}}{1+\frac{b^{2}}{1+b^{2}}}=\dfrac{1}{1+2b^{2}}$,
so $\sqrt{(1-\rho)/(1+\rho)}=1/\sqrt{1+2b^{2}}$, giving @eq-sf-expected-squared-probit. The variance
statement follows by subtracting from the first moment $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(a+bZ)]=\Phi(\lambda)$ of
@prp-agg-probit-closed-form. $\square$
:::

::: {#exm-sf-owen}
## A probit second moment by hand
Take $a=0.5$, $b=1$, so a probit linear predictor $\eta=0.5+Z$ with $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, that is
$\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0.5,1)$. The first moment is $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\eta)]=\Phi(0.5/\sqrt{2})=\Phi(0.3536)=0.6382$
by @prp-agg-probit-closed-form. For the second moment, $\lambda=0.5/\sqrt{2}=0.3536$ and
$1/\sqrt{1+2}=1/\sqrt3=0.5774$, so by @eq-sf-expected-squared-probit
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\Phi(\eta)^{2}\big]=\Phi(0.3536)-2\,T(0.3536,\,0.5774)=0.6382-2(0.0778)=0.4826 .
$$
The averaged Bernoulli variance is then $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\eta)]-\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\eta)^{2}]=0.6382-0.4826=0.1556$,
and the variance of the probit response itself is
$\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\eta)^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\eta)]^{2}=0.4826-0.6382^{2}=0.4826-0.4073=0.0753$. Both numbers
are exact closed forms in $\Phi$ and $T$; direct numerical integration of
$\int\Phi(0.5+z)^{2}\phi(z)\,dz$ returns $0.4826$, confirming the identity. The Owen value itself is
reproducible with standard tools: a Simpson's rule on the definition integral
$T(h,a)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{a} e^{-\frac12 h^{2}(1+x^{2})}/(1+x^{2})\,dx$ over $[0,0.5774]$ returns
$0.0778$, as does the `T.Owen` function of the R package `sn`. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Probit approximations to the logistic function {#sec-sf-probit-logit}

The logit aggregation integral $J(m,\tau)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{expit}(m+\sqrt\tau\,Z)]$ of @eq-agg-logit-integral
has no elementary closed form (@thm-logit-no-closed-form), whereas its probit sibling does, by the Gaussian
probit integral @eq-limits-probit-integral. This asymmetry invites a strategy: approximate the logistic
inverse-link $\mathrm{expit}$ by one or two probit terms, for each of which the aggregation integral
collapses to a $\Phi$, and obtain a fast explicit approximation to $J$. We derive both the one-probit and
the two-probit approximation.

The two approximations share an exact representation that makes their structure transparent. The standard
logistic distribution is a scale mixture of normals: there is a probability density $w(s)$ on $(0,\infty)$
with $\mathrm{expit}(z)=\int_0^\infty\Phi(z/s)\,w(s)\,ds$. Approximating this mixture by a one-point or
two-point rule, $\mathrm{expit}(z)\approx\sum_{i}\omega_i\Phi(\kappa_i z)$ with $\kappa_i=1/s_i$, is exactly
the one-probit and two-probit construction. The mixture is motivation for the *shape* only, a positively
weighted sum of probits; the density $w(s)$ is never needed, and the numbers below are not read off $w$ by
quadrature but come from Taylor matching. We pin the nodes and weights not from $w$ directly but from the
equivalent and elementary requirement that the approximation match the Taylor expansion of $\mathrm{expit}$
at the origin. The expansion, obtained from $\mathrm{expit}(z)=\tfrac12\big(1+\tanh(z/2)\big)$ and the
series $\tanh(x)=x-\tfrac{x^{3}}{3}+\tfrac{2x^{5}}{15}-\cdots$, is
$$
\mathrm{expit}(z)=\tfrac12+\tfrac{1}{4}z-\tfrac{1}{48}z^{3}+\tfrac{1}{480}z^{5}-\cdots,
$$ {#eq-sf-expit-taylor}
an odd function of $z$ about the value $\tfrac12$. The probit term has the matching odd expansion
$\Phi(\kappa z)-\tfrac12=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\big(\kappa z-\tfrac{(\kappa z)^{3}}{6}+\tfrac{(\kappa z)^{5}}{40}-\cdots\big)$,
from @eq-sf-erf-series through @eq-sf-erf-phi.

::: {#thm-probit-logit-approximation}
## One-probit approximation and one-probit logit aggregation
Let $\kappa=\sqrt{\pi/8}=0.62666\ldots$ Then $\mathrm{expit}(z)\approx\Phi(\kappa z)$ is the unique
one-probit approximation matching $\mathrm{expit}$ in value, first derivative, and second derivative at
$z=0$; the constant $\kappa$ is fixed by the slope condition
$$
\kappa\,\phi(0)=\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\mathrm{expit}'(0)=\frac14 .
$$ {#eq-sf-one-probit-kappa}
Substituting into the logit aggregation integral and applying the Gaussian probit integral
@eq-limits-probit-integral gives the explicit one-probit aggregate
$$
J(m,\tau)=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{expit}(m+\sqrt\tau\,Z)\big]
\approx\Phi\!\Big(\frac{\kappa\,m}{\sqrt{1+\kappa^{2}\tau}}\Big).
$$ {#eq-sf-one-probit-aggregate}
:::

::: {.proof}
Both $\mathrm{expit}(z)-\tfrac12$ and $\Phi(\kappa z)-\tfrac12$ are odd, so they automatically agree in
value at $0$ (both $\tfrac12$) and in every even derivative (all zero); matching is therefore a condition on
the odd derivatives. The first-derivative match requires $\frac{d}{dz}\Phi(\kappa z)\big|_0=\kappa\phi(0)$
to equal $\mathrm{expit}'(0)=\mathrm{expit}(0)(1-\mathrm{expit}(0))=\tfrac14$. Since $\phi(0)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}$,
this is $\kappa/\sqrt{2\pi}=\tfrac14$, that is $\kappa=\sqrt{2\pi}/4=\sqrt{\pi/8}$, which is
@eq-sf-one-probit-kappa; the second-derivative match is the vacuous identity $0=0$. For the aggregate,
write $\eta=m+\sqrt\tau\,Z$ with $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and substitute the approximation:
$$
J(m,\tau)\approx\mathbb{E}\big[\Phi(\kappa\,\eta)\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[\Phi(\kappa m+\kappa\sqrt\tau\,Z)\big]
=\Phi\!\Big(\frac{\kappa m}{\sqrt{1+\kappa^{2}\tau}}\Big),
$$
applying @eq-limits-probit-integral with $a=\kappa m$, $b=\kappa\sqrt\tau$, and $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$,
for which $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(a+bZ)]=\Phi(a/\sqrt{1+b^{2}})$. This is @eq-sf-one-probit-aggregate. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Accuracy and an alternative constant.** The slope-matched one-probit approximation
$\mathrm{expit}(z)\approx\Phi(\sqrt{\pi/8}\,z)$ has maximum absolute error $0.0177$ over all $z$, attained
in the shoulders near $|z|\approx 2.8$. If instead one minimizes the maximum error over $z$ rather than
matching the slope, the optimal constant is $\kappa^{\star}\approx 0.5876$, with maximum error $0.0095$;
this $\kappa^\star$ is the value tabulated in the logistic-versus-normal literature. The slope-matched
$\kappa=\sqrt{\pi/8}$ is the natural choice for aggregation because it makes the approximation exact to
second order at the center of the covariate distribution, where most of the integrating mass of
@eq-sf-one-probit-aggregate sits, and because it is the constant used in @thm-logit-no-closed-form. The
substitution is an approximation, not an identity; ML-NMR fits use exact numerical integration
(@thm-hypercube-integration), and the probit form serves as a fast initializer and analytic check.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

A single probit cannot reproduce the heavier tails of the logistic, which is the source of the residual
$0.0177$ error. A second probit term, with its own scale, corrects the next odd order.

::: {#prp-two-probit-logit}
## Two-probit approximation and two-probit logit aggregation
Seek $\mathrm{expit}(z)\approx\omega_1\Phi(\kappa_1 z)+\omega_2\Phi(\kappa_2 z)$ with
$\omega_1+\omega_2=1$. Matching the Taylor coefficients @eq-sf-expit-taylor at orders $1$, $3$, and $5$
gives the moment conditions
$$
\sum_{i}\omega_i\kappa_i=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{4},\qquad
\sum_{i}\omega_i\kappa_i^{3}=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{8},\qquad
\sum_{i}\omega_i\kappa_i^{5}=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12},
$$ {#eq-sf-two-probit-moments}
whose solution is
$$
\omega_1=0.7371,\quad\kappa_1=0.5191,\qquad
\omega_2=0.2629,\quad\kappa_2=0.9282 .
$$ {#eq-sf-two-probit-coeffs}
The resulting approximation has maximum absolute error $0.0040$, a fourfold improvement on the one-probit
rule, and yields the explicit two-probit aggregate
$$
J(m,\tau)\approx\sum_{i=1}^{2}\omega_i\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{\kappa_i\,m}{\sqrt{1+\kappa_i^{2}\tau}}\Big).
$$ {#eq-sf-two-probit-aggregate}
:::

::: {.proof}
With $\omega_1+\omega_2=1$ the approximation is automatically exact in value at $0$. Subtracting $\tfrac12$
from both sides and equating the odd Taylor coefficients of
$\sum_i\omega_i\big(\Phi(\kappa_i z)-\tfrac12\big)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_i\omega_i\big(\kappa_i z-\tfrac{\kappa_i^{3}z^{3}}{6}+\tfrac{\kappa_i^{5}z^{5}}{40}-\cdots\big)$
with those of @eq-sf-expit-taylor: the $z^{1}$ coefficient gives
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_i\omega_i\kappa_i=\tfrac14$; the $z^{3}$ coefficient gives
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_i\omega_i\kappa_i^{3}/6=\tfrac{1}{48}$; and the $z^{5}$ coefficient gives
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_i\omega_i\kappa_i^{5}/40=\tfrac{1}{480}$. Clearing constants gives the three
conditions @eq-sf-two-probit-moments. Together with $\omega_2=1-\omega_1$ this is a system of three
equations in the three unknowns $(\omega_1,\kappa_1,\kappa_2)$; solving it numerically yields
@eq-sf-two-probit-coeffs. This is a numerical construction, not a hand derivation: the system is nonlinear,
one solves it with a standard root finder (for example Newton's method seeded near the one-probit constant
$\kappa=\sqrt{\pi/8}$), and the real solution with $0<\kappa_1<\kappa_2$ is unique up to swapping the two
labels. Substituting back confirms the three moment equations to the displayed
precision. The maximum-error claim is verified by evaluating
$|\mathrm{expit}(z)-\omega_1\Phi(\kappa_1 z)-\omega_2\Phi(\kappa_2 z)|$ on a fine grid, where the supremum
is $0.0040$. The aggregate @eq-sf-two-probit-aggregate follows by linearity of expectation and applying
@eq-sf-one-probit-aggregate to each term: with the approximation in hand,
$J(m,\tau)\approx\sum_i\omega_i\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\kappa_i\eta)]=\sum_i\omega_i\Phi\big(\kappa_i m/\sqrt{1+\kappa_i^{2}\tau}\big)$. $\square$
:::

::: {#exm-sf-probit-logit}
## Approximating the worked logit integral of Chapter 22
The QMC worked example @exm-qmc-logit evaluates $J(0.5,1)=\int\mathrm{expit}(0.5+x)\phi(x)\,dx$, with
high-accuracy reference value $0.6020$. The one-probit aggregate @eq-sf-one-probit-aggregate gives, with
$\kappa=0.62666$ and $\kappa^{2}=0.39270$,
$$
J(0.5,1)\approx\Phi\!\Big(\frac{0.62666\cdot 0.5}{\sqrt{1+0.39270}}\Big)
=\Phi\!\Big(\frac{0.31333}{1.18014}\Big)=\Phi(0.26550)=0.6047,
$$
an error of $+0.0027$. The two-probit aggregate @eq-sf-two-probit-aggregate gives
$$
J(0.5,1)\approx 0.7371\,\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac{0.5191\cdot0.5}{\sqrt{1+0.2695}}\Big)
+0.2629\,\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac{0.9282\cdot0.5}{\sqrt{1+0.8616}}\Big)
=0.7371\,\Phi(0.23036)+0.2629\,\Phi(0.34015)=0.6021,
$$
an error of $+0.0001$, an order of magnitude smaller and indistinguishable from the QMC reference at the
precision a health technology assessment reports. The two-probit closed form thus reproduces, with two
evaluations of $\Phi$, the integral that @sec-qmc-example computes with a Sobol' net. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Two different error scales.** The maximum errors quoted above, $0.0177$ for one probit and $0.0040$ for
two, are worst-case errors in $\mathrm{expit}(z)$ itself, pointwise on the probability scale and before any
averaging. The error that actually matters for a fitted model is the error in the aggregate $J(m,\tau)$ after
integrating over the covariate distribution, and it is typically smaller, because the pointwise overshoots
and undershoots partly cancel under the average. The worked example makes this concrete: the one-probit
pointwise maximum is $0.0177$, yet the one-probit aggregate error at $J(0.5,1)$ is only $0.0027$, and the
two-probit aggregate error is $0.0001$. One caveat runs the other way. The matching is done at the center
$z=0$, so the approximation is at its best for event probabilities near $\tfrac12$ and least accurate in the
shoulders, which is worth remembering when the linear predictor sits far in a tail. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Sobol' sequences and the radical inverse {#sec-sf-sobol}

The Sobol' point set of @def-sobol-net is built coordinate by coordinate from a single arithmetic
operation on the index $n$: the radical inverse, which reflects the base-$b$ digits of $n$ about the radix
point. We define it, prove the exact equidistribution that makes its one-dimensional version (the van der
Corput sequence) a low-discrepancy sequence, and then give the digital construction of the full Sobol'
sequence through generating matrices over the field $\mathbb{F}_2$, of which the radical inverse is the
identity-matrix case.

*Why quasi-Monte Carlo at all.* The aggregation integrals of Part V are averages over a covariate
distribution, and the honest way to compute a $d$-dimensional average with no closed form is to sample points
and average the integrand. Independent random points (plain Monte Carlo) give a root-mean-square error of
order $N^{-1/2}$ in the number of points $N$ (@thm-mc-rmse): to halve the error you must quadruple the
sample. Sobol' points are chosen deterministically to be spread out rather than random, and they achieve an
error of order $(\log N)^{d}/N$ for integrands of bounded Hardy-Krause variation
(@thm-hypercube-integration), which for a fixed dimension beats $N^{-1/2}$ for all large $N$. In the low dimensions typical once ML-NMR reduces to a handful of effect-modifying covariates,
this is often an order-of-magnitude gain at the same $N$, which is why the model integrates with Sobol'
points and not random ones.

*What to retain, and what software handles.* The rest of this section proves why the construction works, and
it uses the vocabulary of digital nets: the field $\mathbb{F}_2=\{0,1\}$ with arithmetic modulo $2$ (where
addition is the exclusive-or, $1\oplus1=0$), generating matrices, direction numbers, and primitive
polynomials. For applied ML-NMR work almost none of this needs to be carried in the head. What to retain is
the applied picture: Sobol' points fill the unit cube evenly, leaving no large empty region, so that after
the inverse-CDF and copula transforms of Chapter 22 the covariate space is covered without gaps. The
generating-matrix algebra below is implementation detail that established libraries, with the tabulated
direction numbers of Joe and Kuo, handle once and for all. Read the proofs for understanding; you need not
reimplement them. Finally, the same point set serves every Part V integrand without change: the integrand may
be a mean (Chapter 20), a Bernoulli or binomial likelihood contribution, a censored survival likelihood
$h^{\delta}S$, or an ordinal category probability (Chapter 25). The dimension $d$ is the number of integrated
covariates, only the integrand changes, and the Sobol' machinery is the same throughout.

::: {#def-radical-inverse}
## Radical inverse and the van der Corput sequence
Fix an integer base $b\ge 2$. Every nonnegative integer $n$ has a unique finite base-$b$ expansion
$n=\sum_{\ell\ge 0}a_\ell(n)\,b^{\ell}$ with digits $a_\ell(n)\in\{0,1,\dots,b-1\}$. The **radical inverse**
of $n$ in base $b$ is obtained by reflecting these digits about the radix point (the radix point is the
base-$b$ analogue of the decimal point, the marker separating the integer digits from the fractional digits),
$$
\varphi_b(n)=\sum_{\ell\ge 0}a_\ell(n)\,b^{-\ell-1}\in[0,1).
$$ {#eq-sf-radical-inverse}
The **van der Corput sequence** in base $b$ is $\big(\varphi_b(n)\big)_{n\ge 0}$, and its base-$2$ instance
is the first coordinate of the Sobol' sequence. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader's translation.* In base $2$ the index $n=6=(110)_2$ has its digits reflected to $0.011_2=\tfrac14+\tfrac18=\tfrac38$.
Feeding $n=1,2,3,\dots$ through $\varphi_2$ therefore lays down the points $\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac34,\tfrac18,\dots$,
each new one dropped into the largest remaining gap. That is the whole idea of a low-discrepancy sequence:
successive points avoid where the earlier ones already sit.

::: {#prp-radical-inverse-net}
## Exact equidistribution of the radical inverse
Fix $b\ge 2$ and $m\ge 1$, and let $N=b^{m}$. The first $N$ radical-inverse points
$\{\varphi_b(n):0\le n<b^{m}\}$ are exactly the $b^{m}$ left endpoints of the equal subintervals of length
$b^{-m}$,
$$
\big\{\varphi_b(n):0\le n<b^{m}\big\}=\Big\{0,\ \tfrac{1}{b^{m}},\ \tfrac{2}{b^{m}},\ \dots,\ \tfrac{b^{m}-1}{b^{m}}\Big\}.
$$ {#eq-sf-radical-net}
Consequently this point set is a $(0,m,1)$-net in base $b$ in the sense of @def-sobol-net: every elementary
interval $[c\,b^{-d},(c+1)b^{-d})$ with $0\le d\le m$ contains exactly $b^{m-d}$ of the points. Its star
discrepancy (the largest mismatch between the fraction of points inside a box $[0,u)$ and the box's own
length $u$, a single number measuring how unevenly the points are spread) is $D_N^{*}=b^{-m}=1/N$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For $0\le n<b^{m}$ only the digits $a_0(n),\dots,a_{m-1}(n)$ can be nonzero, so by @eq-sf-radical-inverse
$$
\varphi_b(n)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{m-1}a_\ell(n)\,b^{-\ell-1}
=b^{-m}\sum_{\ell=0}^{m-1}a_\ell(n)\,b^{\,m-1-\ell}=\frac{r(n)}{b^{m}},
\qquad r(n):=\sum_{\ell=0}^{m-1}a_\ell(n)\,b^{\,m-1-\ell}.
$$
The map $n\mapsto r(n)$ replaces the digit string $(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{m-1})$ by the integer with reversed
digit string $(a_{m-1},\dots,a_1,a_0)$. Digit reversal is a bijection of the set of $m$-digit base-$b$
strings onto itself, hence $n\mapsto r(n)$ is a bijection of $\{0,1,\dots,b^{m}-1\}$ onto itself. Therefore
$\{\varphi_b(n):0\le n<b^{m}\}=\{r/b^{m}:0\le r<b^{m}\}$, which is @eq-sf-radical-net.

For the net property, an elementary interval $[c\,b^{-d},(c+1)b^{-d})$ of length $b^{-d}$ with $d\le m$ is
the union of exactly $b^{m-d}$ of the grid cells $[r b^{-m},(r+1)b^{-m})$, namely those with
$c\,b^{m-d}\le r<(c+1)b^{m-d}$. Since @eq-sf-radical-net places exactly one point at each grid left
endpoint $r/b^{m}$, the interval contains exactly $b^{m-d}$ points, which is $b^{t}$ with $t=0$; this is the
defining property of a $(0,m,1)$-net (@def-sobol-net). For the star discrepancy, the local discrepancy
$\Delta_N(u)=\frac1N\#\{n:\varphi_b(n)<u\}-u$ of the grid $\{r/N\}$ satisfies, for
$u\in\big(\tfrac{j}{N},\tfrac{j+1}{N}\big]$, $\#\{r/N<u\}=j+1$ (the points $0,\tfrac1N,\dots,\tfrac jN$), so
$\Delta_N(u)=\tfrac{j+1}{N}-u\in\big[0,\tfrac1N\big)$, approaching $\tfrac1N$ as $u\downarrow j/N$; hence
$D_N^{*}=\sup_u|\Delta_N(u)|=1/N$ (@def-star-discrepancy). $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**From the exact net to the sequence rate.** @prp-radical-inverse-net controls the point set of size
exactly $N=b^{m}$. For an arbitrary truncation length $N$, not a power of $b$, the van der Corput sequence
has star discrepancy $D_N^{*}=O\big((\log N)/N\big)$, the one-dimensional low-discrepancy rate; the proof
decomposes $N$ into its base-$b$ digits and applies the exact-net bound on each dyadic block, the $\log N$
factor counting the blocks. This is the $d=1$ case of the Sobol' rate $D_N^{*}=O((\log N)^{d}/N)$ quoted in
@def-sobol-net, and it is realized in the seven-point worked example below. The contrast with the $N^{-1/2}$
spread of independent uniform points (@thm-mc-rmse) is the quasi-Monte Carlo advantage. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The full Sobol' sequence replaces the digit-reversal of @eq-sf-radical-inverse, which is multiplication of
the digit vector by the identity matrix, with multiplication by a carefully chosen matrix over
$\mathbb{F}_2=\{0,1\}$, a different matrix per coordinate. This is the digital construction.

::: {#def-sobol-construction}
## Digital nets and the Sobol' generating matrices
Work in base $b=2$ and identify a point $u\in[0,1)$ with its binary digit vector
$u=\sum_{k\ge 1}y_k 2^{-k}$, $y_k\in\mathbb{F}_2$. For each coordinate $i=1,\dots,s$ fix a **generating
matrix** $C_i\in\mathbb{F}_2^{\,w\times w}$ (entries in $\mathbb{F}_2$, with $w$ the working bit depth). The
$i$-th coordinate of the $n$-th digital point is defined by carrying the binary digits of $n$ through
$C_i$ with arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_2$: writing $n=\sum_{\ell\ge 0}a_\ell(n)2^{\ell}$ and
$\mathbf{a}(n)=(a_0(n),a_1(n),\dots)^\top$,
$$
\mathbf{y}^{(i)}=C_i\,\mathbf{a}(n)\ \ (\text{mod }2),\qquad
u_{n,i}=\sum_{k\ge 1}y^{(i)}_k\,2^{-k}.
$$ {#eq-sf-digital-point}
Taking $C_i=I$ (the identity) recovers the radical inverse $u_{n,i}=\varphi_2(n)$ of @eq-sf-radical-inverse.
The **Sobol' sequence** is the digital sequence whose $i$-th generating matrix $C_i$ has, as its columns,
the binary expansions of the **direction numbers** $v_{i,\ell}=m_{i,\ell}2^{-\ell}$ (a fixed list of dyadic
fractions, one per bit level $\ell$, that encodes how coordinate $i$ is scrambled) generated from a
**primitive polynomial** over $\mathbb{F}_2$ (an irreducible polynomial whose root generates every nonzero
element of a binary field, the standard device for producing a maximal-length binary recurrence) by the
recurrence of @eq-qmc-sobol-point; with that choice @eq-sf-digital-point reproduces
$u_{n,i}=\bigoplus_{\ell:\,a_\ell(n)=1}v_{i,\ell}$, the exclusive-or of the selected direction numbers.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-sf-digital-2d}
## A four-point digital net in two dimensions
The smallest example that shows "balanced in every box" beyond one dimension uses base $2$, resolution $m=2$,
and $s=2$ coordinates, so $N=2^{2}=4$ points. Take the first coordinate to be the radical inverse,
$C_1=I_2$, and the second to be generated by
$$
C_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\ \ (\text{over }\mathbb{F}_2).
$$
Running $n=0,1,2,3$ with index bits $\mathbf{a}(n)=(a_0,a_1)^\top$ through @eq-sf-digital-point gives the
four points
$$
(0,0),\quad\Big(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\Big),\quad\Big(\tfrac14,\tfrac34\Big),\quad\Big(\tfrac34,\tfrac14\Big).
$$
This set is a $(0,2,2)$-net: every elementary box of area $2^{-2}=\tfrac14$ holds exactly one point. There
are three shapes of such box, one per split $(d_1,d_2)$ of the two available resolution levels. The four
vertical quarter-strips $[j/4,(j+1)/4)\times[0,1)$ each catch one point, because the $x$-coordinates are the
four distinct quarters $\{0,\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac34\}$; the four horizontal strips likewise, because the
$y$-coordinates are the same four quarters; and the four half-by-half boxes each catch one, as one checks by
listing: $(0,0)$ and $(\tfrac14,\tfrac34)$ lie in the left half, $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and $(\tfrac34,\tfrac14)$
in the right, with one high and one low in each. No box of area $\tfrac14$ is empty and none holds two: that
is exactly the even coverage the rank condition of @prp-digital-net-rank guarantees, here because the row
stack $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ of the first row of $C_1$ over the first
row of $C_2$, together with $C_1$ and $C_2$ themselves, are each full rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-digital-net-rank}
## The digital-net equidistribution condition
Let a base-$2$ digital point set $\{(u_{n,1},\dots,u_{n,s}):0\le n<2^{m}\}$ be generated by matrices
$C_1,\dots,C_s\in\mathbb{F}_2^{\,m\times m}$ as in @eq-sf-digital-point (using the low-order $m$ bits). The
set is a $(t,m,s)$-net in base $2$ (every elementary interval of volume $2^{t-m}$ holds exactly $2^{t}$
points) provided that for every choice of nonnegative integers $d_1,\dots,d_s$ with
$d_1+\cdots+d_s=m-t$, the $(m-t)\times m$ matrix obtained by stacking the **first $d_i$ rows** of each $C_i$
has rank $m-t$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$. For $s=1$ and $C_1=I$ the condition holds with $t=0$, recovering
@prp-radical-inverse-net.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove the rank condition is sufficient; the $s=1$ identity case is then immediate and is exactly
@prp-radical-inverse-net. Fix $d_1,\dots,d_s$ with $\sum_i d_i=m-t$ and consider the elementary interval
$$
E=\prod_{i=1}^{s}\big[c_i\,2^{-d_i},(c_i+1)2^{-d_i}\big),\qquad 0\le c_i<2^{d_i},
$$
of volume $2^{-(d_1+\cdots+d_s)}=2^{t-m}$. The condition $u_{n,i}\in[c_i 2^{-d_i},(c_i+1)2^{-d_i})$
constrains exactly the leading $d_i$ binary digits $y^{(i)}_1,\dots,y^{(i)}_{d_i}$ of the $i$-th coordinate
to equal the binary digits of $c_i$. By @eq-sf-digital-point each such digit $y^{(i)}_k$ is the inner
product over $\mathbb{F}_2$ of the $k$-th row of $C_i$ with the index vector $\mathbf{a}(n)\in\mathbb{F}_2^{m}$.
Collecting the $\sum_i d_i=m-t$ constrained digits over all coordinates gives a linear system
$A\,\mathbf{a}(n)=\mathbf{c}\ (\text{mod }2)$, where $A\in\mathbb{F}_2^{(m-t)\times m}$ is precisely the
stack of the first $d_i$ rows of each $C_i$ and $\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{F}_2^{m-t}$ encodes the box
$(c_1,\dots,c_s)$. By hypothesis $\mathrm{rank}(A)=m-t$, so $A$ is surjective and the solution set
$\{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{F}_2^{m}:A\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{c}\}$ is an affine subspace of dimension
$m-(m-t)=t$, containing exactly $2^{t}$ vectors. As $n$ ranges over $\{0,\dots,2^{m}-1\}$ the index vector
$\mathbf{a}(n)$ ranges over all of $\mathbb{F}_2^{m}$ bijectively, so exactly $2^{t}$ indices $n$ land in
$E$. Since the box $E$ was an arbitrary elementary interval of volume $2^{t-m}$, the point set is a
$(t,m,s)$-net (@def-sobol-net). For $s=1$, $C_1=I_m$: any single $d_1=m$ selects the first $m$ rows of $I_m$,
which is $I_m$, of rank $m=m-0$, so $t=0$ and the net is $(0,m,1)$, as in @prp-radical-inverse-net. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the rank condition buys, and where Sobol' directions come from.** @prp-digital-net-rank reduces the
geometric demand of low discrepancy, exact balance in every dyadic box, to a linear-algebra demand on the
generating matrices, full rank of every admissible row-stack over $\mathbb{F}_2$. The art of constructing a
good Sobol' sequence is choosing the direction numbers so that the resulting matrices $C_i$ keep the net
quality parameter $t$ small simultaneously across many coordinates and many resolutions $m$; the primitive-
polynomial recurrence of @eq-qmc-sobol-point guarantees full rank within each single coordinate, and the
tabulated initial direction numbers of Joe and Kuo (2008) optimize the joint two-dimensional projections.
The whole apparatus serves the one purpose of @thm-hypercube-integration: a point set whose star
discrepancy attains $O((\log N)^{d}/N)$, so that the Koksma-Hlawka bound @thm-koksma-hlawka delivers
near-$1/N$ integration error for the aggregation integral whenever the pulled-back integrand has finite
Hardy-Krause variation (Chapter 22 records when it does not). The same statement carries over when the
integrand is a survival or ordinal likelihood kernel rather than a mean, which is the setting of Chapter 25:
the points and the bound do not know what they are integrating. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-sf-vandercorput}
## The seven-point van der Corput set
Take $b=2$ and list $\varphi_2(n)$ for $n=1,\dots,7$ by reflecting binary digits about the radix point:
$n=1=(1)_2\mapsto 0.1_2=\tfrac12$; $n=2=(10)_2\mapsto 0.01_2=\tfrac14$; $n=3=(11)_2\mapsto 0.11_2=\tfrac34$;
$n=4=(100)_2\mapsto 0.001_2=\tfrac18$; and likewise $\tfrac58,\tfrac38,\tfrac78$ for $n=5,6,7$. As a set
this is $\{\tfrac18,\tfrac28,\tfrac38,\tfrac48,\tfrac58,\tfrac68,\tfrac78\}$, the seven interior eighths,
matching the worked Sobol' example of @sec-qmc-sobol. Its star discrepancy is $D_7^{*}=\tfrac18$: the
largest gap between the empirical fraction $\frac1N\#\{\varphi_2(n)<u\}$ and $u$ occurs as $u\uparrow k/8$,
where the fraction is $\frac{k-1}{7}$ against the volume $\frac{k}{8}$, and the maximum of
$\big|\frac{k}{8}-\frac{k-1}{7}\big|$ over $k=1,\dots,7$ is $\tfrac18$ at $k=1$ (the same value is approached
as $u\downarrow\tfrac78$, where the fraction is $1$ against $\tfrac78$). This is close to $1/N$ and
far below the $1/\sqrt7\approx 0.38$ typical of seven independent uniform draws, the discrepancy gap that
@prp-radical-inverse-net explains and that drives the QMC error advantage of @thm-hypercube-integration.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-sf-notes}

The moment generating function and the normal MGF @eq-sf-normal-mgf are developed in Chapter 4
(@def-mgf, @def-mvn, @eq-mvn-mgf); the log-link aggregation corollary @cor-sf-log-link restates
@thm-log-link-mgf of Chapter 20 (catalogue H.6), whose proof is the same MGF-at-$t=1$ computation. The
log-normal mean $\mathbb{E}[e^{W}]=e^{m+v/2}$ is classical. The error function and its relation to $\Phi$
are standard special-function material; the series @eq-sf-erf-series and the asymptotic expansion
@eq-sf-erfc-asymptotic, with the Mills ratio $1-\Phi(x)\sim\phi(x)/x$, are in Abramowitz and Stegun,
*Handbook of Mathematical Functions* (Chapter 7), and the integration-by-parts derivation given here is the
textbook one.

Owen's $T$ function, its tables, and the bivariate normal probability reduction @eq-sf-owen-general are due
to @owen1956; the function @eq-sf-owens-t-def and the wedge representation @eq-sf-owens-t-prob are his. The
correlation heat equation @eq-sf-biv-pde for the bivariate normal density is Plackett's identity (R. L.
Plackett, *Biometrika* 1954); the differentiate-in-$\rho$ proof of the diagonal identity
@eq-sf-owens-t-identity is the standard route and is given here in full. The expected-squared-probit
identity @eq-sf-expected-squared-probit is the second-moment companion of the probit aggregation result
@prp-agg-probit-closed-form of Chapter 20, which is itself the Gaussian probit integral
@lem-limits-probit-integral of Chapter 16; the conditioning argument $\Phi(a+bZ)=P(U\le a+bZ\mid Z)$ is the
same device used there.

The probit approximations to the logistic function have a long history in psychometrics and in the
logistic-versus-probit literature. The slope-matched constant $\kappa=\sqrt{\pi/8}$ of
@thm-probit-logit-approximation is the one quoted in @thm-logit-no-closed-form; the maximum-error-optimal
constant $\kappa^\star\approx 0.5876=1/1.702$ noted in the remark is the scaling constant of item response
theory, usually attributed to Haley (1952). The scale-mixture viewpoint underlying the
two-probit construction @prp-two-probit-logit, that the logistic distribution is a Gaussian scale mixture
and that a two-point quadrature of the mixing law yields a sum of two probits, follows Monahan and
Stefanski (in *Handbook of the Logistic Distribution*, 1992); the coefficients @eq-sf-two-probit-coeffs are
derived here by Taylor matching and verified numerically, and the two-probit aggregate
@eq-sf-two-probit-aggregate reproduces the Chapter 22 worked integral @exm-qmc-logit to four decimals.

The radical inverse @eq-sf-radical-inverse and the van der Corput sequence are the base case of the
low-discrepancy theory of Chapter 22; the exact-equidistribution result @prp-radical-inverse-net and its
$(0,m,1)$-net reading are elementary and self-contained here, and the general digital-net rank condition
@prp-digital-net-rank is the base-$2$ case of Niederreiter's theory of $(t,m,s)$-nets (Niederreiter,
*Random Number Generation and Quasi-Monte Carlo Methods*, 1992, Chapter 4). The Sobol' construction
@def-sobol-construction, the direction-number recurrence, and the discrepancy rate are from @sobol1967, with
the modern direction tables of Joe and Kuo (2008); the construction is consistent with @def-sobol-net of
Chapter 22, of which it is the generating-matrix formulation. None of the special-function material of this
appendix is part of the Coq development, which formalizes the population-adjustment and causal core of the
book and not the numerical-integration theory; no machine-checked tags are claimed.
